parts.title: Joining a Car-Share Club
parts.scenario: A woman phones a city car-share club to become a member.

voices.label: Narrator
voices.desc: Test narrator — neutral, clear, measured British RP; the same voice in every test

voices.label: Craig
voices.desc: Membership officer — male, 30s, easy-going, helpful, slightly chatty; Australian accent

voices.label: Joanna
voices.desc: Caller — female, late 20s, friendly, organised but a little hurried; Australian accent

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning a car-share club to become a member. First, you have some time to look at Questions 1 to 7.

script.speaker: Craig
script.text: [telephone rings twice, then the line clicks open] [cheerful, professional] Harbour Car Share, Craig speaking. How can I help?

script.speaker: Joanna
script.text: [friendly, slightly hurried] Oh, hi, Craig. I'd like to join the club, please. The online form kept freezing on me, so I thought I'd just ring.

script.speaker: Craig
script.text: [apologetic chuckle] Yeah, sorry about that. No worries, I can do it over the phone. Can I start with your name?

script.speaker: Joanna
script.text: Sure. It's Joanna Pellowe.

script.speaker: Craig
script.text: [careful] And how do you spell the surname?

script.speaker: Joanna
script.text: [slowly, spelling each letter clearly] P... E... double L... O... W... E.

script.speaker: Craig
script.text: [reading back as he types] P... E... double L... O... W...

script.speaker: Joanna
script.text: [quickly, politely correcting him] Sorry, there's an E on the end as well. People always leave it off.

script.speaker: Craig
script.text: [light laugh] Got it, with the E. And your home address?

script.speaker: Joanna
script.text: [clearly] It's flat six, forty-two Lennox Street, in Rozelle.

script.speaker: Craig
script.text: [murmuring as he types] Lennox Street... [normal voice] and the postcode?

script.speaker: Joanna
script.text: [thinking] Two-oh-three-nine... [short pause] [correcting herself, a bit embarrassed] no, hang on, that's the office. Home is two-oh-three-seven.

script.speaker: Craig
script.text: [reading back slowly] Two-oh-three-seven. Lovely. Now, we ask everyone what they'll mainly be using the cars for. Is it mostly for work, or...?

script.speaker: Joanna
script.text: [thoughtful] Not for work, no. I cycle to the office. I used to borrow a friend's car to take my sister to the airport, but she's moved to Perth now, so... [warmly] these days it'd mostly be to drive up and see my grandmother. She lives in a little town in the Blue Mountains, and the train doesn't go all the way.

script.speaker: Craig
script.text: [sympathetic] Yeah, the trains up there aren't great at weekends. And which of our car bays would be handiest for you? In Rozelle we've got three.

script.speaker: Joanna
script.text: [considering] Well, the one at the light rail stop would be ideal, but every time I've looked on the map, the cars there are booked out.

script.speaker: Craig
script.text: [rueful] That one's very popular, I'm afraid.

script.speaker: Joanna
script.text: [thinking aloud] And the bay outside the library, I thought that'd be the closest, but...

script.speaker: Craig
script.text: [helpful] Ah, that one's actually closed till the end of the year. The council's digging up the road there.

script.speaker: Joanna
script.text: [decisive] Right, then put me down for the one behind the swimming pool. It's only a five-minute walk, so that's fine.

script.speaker: Craig
script.text: [typing] Behind the pool, no problem. You can change that any time in the app anyway. [explaining, clear] Now, we've got three plans. There's Casual, which has no monthly fee but higher hourly rates; there's Plus, which has a small monthly fee and cheaper hours; and Premium, which is really for people who drive most days.

script.speaker: Joanna
script.text: [hesitant] I was thinking Casual, because I honestly won't drive that much. Maybe twice a month?

script.speaker: Craig
script.text: [measured, reasoning it through] You could. But two return trips to the mountains a month, they're long bookings, say six or seven hours each. On Casual you'd be paying the higher rate the whole time. I reckon the middle one would work out cheaper for you.

script.speaker: Joanna
script.text: [doing the maths slowly] Hmm... yeah, if they're full-day trips... [decisive] Okay, you've talked me into it. I'll go for Plus. Not Premium, though, that's way more than I need.

script.speaker: Craig
script.text: [laughs] Fair enough. Plus it is.

script.speaker: Joanna
script.text: And what's the monthly fee on that? The website said twelve dollars fifty.

script.speaker: Craig
script.text: [apologetic] Ah, that's last year's figure, the page hasn't been updated. It went up in July. It's fourteen dollars ninety-five a month now.

script.speaker: Joanna
script.text: [resigned, good-humoured] Fourteen ninety-five. Okay. Still a lot cheaper than running my own car.

script.speaker: Craig
script.text: [businesslike] Definitely. Now, we'll need a scan of your driver's licence, front and back, and something showing your address. A bank statement's fine...

script.speaker: Joanna
script.text: [awkward] I don't get paper statements any more. It's all online, and the screenshots don't actually show my address.

script.speaker: Craig
script.text: [thinking] Right. We used to take mobile phone bills, but we can't accept those any more, head office changed the rules. Have you got a gas or an electricity bill?

script.speaker: Joanna
script.text: [relieved] The gas is in my flatmate's name, but I can send you my electricity bill, that's got my name and address on it.

script.speaker: Craig
script.text: Perfect. Just email it to us with the licence scan.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at Questions 8 to 10.

script.speaker: Joanna
script.text: [slightly anxious] Can I ask about the rules? What happens if I'm late bringing a car back? The traffic coming down from the mountains can be awful on a Sunday night.

script.speaker: Craig
script.text: [reassuring] It happens. If you can, extend the booking in the app before it runs out. If you don't, there is a charge. It used to be a flat twenty-five dollars, whatever happened, which people thought was a bit harsh if they were only five minutes over.

script.speaker: Joanna
script.text: [wry] I can imagine.

script.speaker: Craig
script.text: [clear, explaining] So now it's worked out in blocks of fifteen minutes. You pay a small fee for each block you're over. [emphatic] We don't charge you for a whole extra hour, which is what some of the other clubs do.

script.speaker: Joanna
script.text: [curious] That sounds fairer. And is there anything I have to do before I drive off? Do I need to ring you?

script.speaker: Craig
script.text: [casual] You don't need to call us. That's what we used to ask, but the app does all that now. Some members check the petrol gauge, but honestly, our staff refuel the cars, and there's a fuel card in the glovebox if you do run low, so that's not something you need to worry about.

script.speaker: Joanna
script.text: Oh, right.

script.speaker: Craig
script.text: [more serious, emphatic] The one thing we do insist on is that you walk around the car and take pictures of any scratches or dents in the app. Otherwise you could end up getting blamed for them.

script.speaker: Joanna
script.text: [serious] Good to know. I'll make sure I do that.

script.speaker: Craig
script.text: [upbeat] So, would you like to make your first booking now? Your membership card takes about five days to come in the post.

script.speaker: Joanna
script.text: [hesitant] Oh, so I'd have to wait for that anyway?

script.speaker: Craig
script.text: [quickly] No, no, you don't need the card. Once your documents are approved, you can unlock the cars with your phone. That's usually the same day.

script.speaker: Joanna
script.text: [pleased] Oh, good. I was hoping to go up this Saturday.

script.speaker: Craig
script.text: [checking, murmuring] Let me see... [normal voice] yep, the hatchback behind the pool is free all day Saturday.

script.speaker: Joanna
script.text: [thinking aloud, hesitant] Actually... I'd better not book it yet. My grandmother sometimes goes to her bridge club on a Saturday, and I don't want to drive all that way if she isn't going to be home. I'll ring her tonight and then book it in the app.

script.speaker: Craig
script.text: [easy-going] No problem at all. I'll email you a link to the app in the next few minutes.

script.speaker: Joanna
script.text: [warmly] Great. Thanks so much for your help, Craig.

script.speaker: Craig
script.text: [cheerful] My pleasure, Joanna. Enjoy the drive.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: The Ashcombe Heritage Trail
parts.context: Monologue in an everyday social context (local radio talk, with short introduction by a presenter)
parts.scenario: A local radio presenter introduces the council's heritage officer, who describes a new heritage trail in the town.
parts.tool: Text to Speech (presenter introduction + main speaker; one voice per label)

voices.label: Narrator
voices.desc: Test narrator — neutral, clear, measured British RP; the same voice in every test

voices.label: Presenter
voices.desc: Local radio presenter — male, 40s, warm, upbeat, polished; British accent

voices.label: Ruth
voices.desc: Council heritage officer — female, 50s, enthusiastic, articulate, occasionally wry; British (southern English) accent

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a local radio presenter introducing a heritage officer, who is talking about a new heritage trail in her town. First, you have some time to look at Questions 11 to 16.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: [radio studio, a short jingle fading out] [warm, lively] Good morning, and welcome back to Ashcombe Today. Now, those small metal discs that have appeared in the town centre pavements are part of the new Ashcombe Heritage Trail, which opens this Saturday, and here to tell us all about it is the council's heritage officer, Ruth Penhale. Morning, Ruth.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: [cheerful] Morning, Steve, and thanks for having me. [settling in, enthusiastic] Well, the trail links fourteen places of interest in the old town, but this morning I'll just pick out six of the main ones.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: [informative] Let's start at the Corn Exchange on the High Street. A lot of people still think of it as the place to get a coffee, and there was a café on the ground floor for years, but it closed last spring and the space is empty for now. What you will find just inside the entrance hall is a model of the town as it looked in about eighteen fifty. [warm] It was built by pupils from Ashcombe Primary as a class project last term, and it's remarkably detailed. They even put tiny sheep in the market square.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: [slightly regretful] From there, the trail goes down Well Lane to St Bride's Well. This is one of the oldest sites in the town; there's been a spring there since medieval times. We'd originally planned to put one of our audio posts there, where you press a button and hear a short recording, but the budget didn't stretch that far, sadly.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: [careful, serious] And I should warn listeners: the well sits at the bottom of a flight of very narrow, uneven steps. We did look into putting in a ramp, but because the stonework is protected, we weren't given permission. So I'm afraid it isn't a stop that anyone in a wheelchair will be able to get down to.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: [brighter] Just past the well, you come to the Tannery Bridge over the river. Now, generations of Ashcombe people have called it the black bridge, because that's the colour it's been for as long as anyone can remember. But when our conservation team scraped back the layers of paint last year, they discovered the ironwork had first been painted a deep green, and that's the shade you'll see there now. [light laugh] It's caused a few complaints, actually.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: [informative] Then it's back up the hill to the Market Cross. You'll see people climbing the steps around the base hoping for a view, but to be honest, you can't see much from there; the buildings are too close. What makes the cross special is the bell at the top. The original was stolen in the nineteen seventies and never recovered. The one hanging there now was cast last year by a foundry in Devon, copied exactly from old photographs.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: [informative, slightly apologetic] Round the corner from the cross are the Weavers' Cottages, a row of five little houses where cloth used to be made by hand. People are often disappointed to learn that they're all private homes now, so you can't just wander in. But the owners of the end cottage have very kindly agreed to let us in once a month, which means the only way to see inside is to book a place on one of our guided walks.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: [enthusiastic] And finally, there's the old Railway Goods Shed, down by the station car park. There's one of our audio posts inside, and if you press the button, you'll hear recordings we made with men and women who worked on the railway in the nineteen fifties and sixties.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: [matter-of-fact] A lot of people ask me whether there's somewhere to eat in the shed. There isn't, I'm afraid, though the Signal Box Café is just over the road. And if you're after a view over the whole town, the best place is really the old water tower behind the station, but that's not part of the trail, because it isn't open to the public.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at Questions 17 to 20.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: [interested] Ruth, tell us about those discs in the pavement.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: [chuckles] Ah, the markers. Well, there was quite a debate about those. Some councillors wanted them made from recycled plastic, to be environmentally friendly, but in the end we went for bronze, because it lasts so much longer. [warm] They were designed by Ellen Marsh, a sculptor who's lived in Ashcombe all her life. They shouldn't need replacing for a very long time; we're hoping they'll still be there in fifty years.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: [practical] As for how long it takes, the leaflet says forty-five minutes, but that's if you walk briskly and don't stop at all. If you actually read the information boards, I'd allow about an hour and a half. Some people make a whole morning of it and have lunch at the end, but that's up to you.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: [advisory] There's also a free app to go with the trail. Some people tell me they prefer it to the printed leaflet, but personally I find the map in the leaflet much easier to follow. There's a paid version of the app with extra content, too, but honestly, the free one has everything most visitors would need.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: [emphatic, slowing down] My main piece of advice is this: the mobile signal in the old streets is terrible. So if you want to use the app, make sure you've got it on your phone before you leave home.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: [curious] And is there any way listeners can get involved?

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: [grateful] Well, we've had a wonderful response to our appeal for volunteer guides. In fact, we've got all the guides we need for this year, so thank you to everyone who came forward. Last year we asked people to suggest buildings to include, and that went well, too.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: [eager, warm] What we're short of now is pictures. If you've got old photographs of the town in a drawer at home, shops, street parties, anything, we'd love to scan them for the trail website. You can drop them at the library, and we'll return them within a week.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: [wrapping up, cheerful] Lovely. Ruth Penhale, thank you very much.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Seminar Presentation: How Young Children Acquire Language
parts.scenario: Two students, Hannah and Liam, prepare a seminar presentation on how young children acquire language.

voices.label: Narrator
voices.desc: Test narrator — neutral, clear, measured British RP; the same voice in every test

voices.label: Hannah
voices.desc: Student — female, early 20s, organised, a little anxious, quick; British (southern English) accent

voices.label: Liam
voices.desc: Student — male, early 20s, relaxed, confident, persuasive; New Zealand accent

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two students, Hannah and Liam, preparing a seminar presentation on how young children acquire language. First, you have some time to look at Questions 21 to 24.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [quiet study room] [brisk, a little stressed] Okay, Liam, we've got twenty minutes for the whole presentation, including questions, so we really need to decide what goes in and what comes out.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [relaxed] Yeah, fair enough. I made a list last night. Shall we go through it?

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: Go on.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [reading from notes] Right, first, Chomsky, and the idea that we're born with some kind of built-in grammar.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [doubtful] Hmm. I mean, it's important, obviously, but everyone in the group did that to death in first year. If we spend five minutes on it, people will just switch off.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [agreeing] True. So we cut it, then. We can mention his name in passing, but not give it a section. [short pause] Next, kids who grow up with two languages.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [hesitant] I was wondering about dropping that, actually. It's such a huge area.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [firm but friendly] Ah, no, I really think we need it. Half the people in our seminar group grew up speaking more than one language at home. They'll want to hear about it.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [conceding] Fair point. Keep it, but keep it short. What's next?

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [enthusiastic] Children learning sign language. There's that brilliant study from Nicaragua.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [regretful] I'd love to include that, but realistically, we'd have to explain how sign languages work first, and we just haven't got the time.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [sighs] Yeah, you're right. It'd need a whole presentation of its own. And what about screen time, whether toddlers pick up words from the television?

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [dismissive] I'd have said drop that, to be honest. The research is pretty thin.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [persuasive] But that's kind of the point, isn't it? Everyone assumes educational programmes help, and the evidence says they mostly don't, not unless an adult is watching and talking about it with the child. That's a nice surprising finding. Just a minute or two.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [laughs] All right, you win. And then babbling, which obviously stays. It's where everything starts.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: Definitely.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [moving on] Okay. Then the main section: child-directed speech. You know, the way adults talk to babies, with the high pitch and the exaggerated tune. Did anything in the reading surprise you?

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [thoughtful] A couple of things. I'd always assumed it was mainly mothers who did it, and that dads sort of talked to babies the same way they talk to anyone else. But that study showed fathers change their voices just as much. That really surprised me.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [interested] Mm. What about the bit showing that newborns would rather listen to it than to normal adult speech? I thought that was amazing, at only a few days old.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [unimpressed, easy] Honestly, that didn't really surprise me. Babies like anything that sounds a bit musical. [more animated] What did get me was that it isn't universal. I'd taken it for granted that every culture does it, but there are communities where adults hardly speak directly to babies at all, and the kids still learn to talk perfectly well.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [agreeing] Yes, that was striking. And older brothers and sisters doing it to toddlers, I found that quite unexpected.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [chuckles] Not me. I've got a four-year-old niece, and she talks to her baby brother exactly like that.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [laughs] Fair enough. And the old claim that it holds back vocabulary?

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [matter-of-fact] Well, nobody really believes that any more. The studies show the opposite, which is pretty much what I'd have expected.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at Questions 25 to 30.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [hesitant] Now, about the video. I was planning to show that clip of my cousin's little boy, the one where he's naming everything in the garden.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [mildly sceptical] It's lovely, but it's nearly ten minutes long, isn't it?

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: Oh, I'd only play a minute of it, I can cut it down easily. And the sound's fine, I recorded it on a decent microphone. [short pause] [sighs] But I've decided not to use it after all. I mentioned it to my cousin, and she wasn't keen on her son being shown to a room full of strangers.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [understanding] No, absolutely, that's her call. We'll find something online instead.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [enthusiastic] Then I want to do the 'wug' experiment. You know, the one where kids are shown a drawing of a made-up creature called a wug, and then two of them, and they have to finish the sentence: 'There are two...'

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [doubtful] Isn't it a bit old, though? It was done in the nineteen fifties.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [firm] It's old, but it hasn't dated at all. I don't think there's anything that shows more clearly that kids aren't just copying what they hear. They've never heard the word 'wugs', so they must be applying a rule.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [hesitant] Some people say the results were overstated, though. That a lot of the kids were just guessing.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [polite but dismissive] I've read that critique, and I don't buy it. The results have been repeated loads of times.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [thinking] Okay. That leads nicely into mistakes like 'I goed' or 'two mouses'.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: Yeah. Parents get really worried about those.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [amused] And they correct them constantly, which, according to everything we read, makes almost no difference.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [agreeing] Right. And people think they've stopped by about four, but actually some kids carry on making them till they're six or seven.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [emphatic] The point we need to get across is that they're not a sign that anything's wrong. It's the reverse, really: the child has worked out the rule and is just using it too widely. That's a step forward.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: Agreed. That's our key message for that section.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [practical] What about a handout? Last time the tutor said ours was far too long.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [thinking] I'd rather not give anything out at the start. People just read it instead of listening.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: We could put all the references on the final slide...

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [doubtful] Nobody can copy down twenty references in the thirty seconds it's up.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [decisive] Okay, so let's email a one-page summary to everyone once the session's over.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: Yes, that's the best option.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [anxious] I'm a bit worried about questions at the end, though. What if someone asks something we can't answer?

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [relaxed] That doesn't bother me. We just say we'll look into it. And we've left five minutes, which is plenty. [more serious] What I'm more concerned about is what happened last term, when we asked for questions and there was total silence. It was so awkward.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [laughs] Oh, I remember. So should we get a friend to ask something?

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [chuckles] Better than that, we'll finish with a question for them to discuss in pairs. That'll get them talking.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [businesslike] Right. So what next? Should we book a meeting with Dr Morgan to check the plan?

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [hesitant] I don't think we need to. She said she's happy as long as we stick to the outline. And we can't really run through it properly till the slides are finished.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [agreeing] True. The problem is, most of our sources are from the nineties. We need some recent research, especially on bilingualism.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [decisive] Okay, let's both spend tomorrow in the library looking for studies from the last five years, and then meet up again on Thursday.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Urban Heat Islands
parts.scenario: A lecturer in urban geography gives a talk on the causes and effects of urban heat islands and on ways of reducing them.

voices.label: Narrator
voices.desc: Test narrator — neutral, clear, measured British RP; the same voice in every test

voices.label: Lecturer
voices.desc: University lecturer in urban geography — female, 40s, energetic, clear, engaging; Canadian accent

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecturer giving a talk about urban heat islands. First, you have some time to look at Questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [lecture hall, a low murmur fading] [warm, energetic] Okay, good afternoon, everyone. Today we're turning to a topic that's become increasingly urgent for city planners, and that's what's known as the urban heat island: the simple fact that cities are often a great deal hotter than the countryside around them.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [explanatory] The difference can be dramatic. In extreme cases, a large city can be as much as twelve degrees warmer than the farmland that surrounds it. [emphatic, slowing down] And here's what surprises most people. The gap isn't at its greatest in the middle of the afternoon, when the sun is strongest. It's widest at night, because the city keeps releasing the heat it has soaked up during the day for hours after sunset, while the countryside cools down quite quickly.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [measured] So what causes it? Well, the first factor is the materials we build with. Dark surfaces like asphalt and roofing tar absorb most of the sunlight that hits them, rather than bouncing it back. Scientists describe this property using the term albedo, that's A... L... B... E... D... O, which is simply a measure of how much light a surface reflects.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [light, illustrative] Fresh snow, for example, has a very high albedo; it sends most of the light back into the sky. Asphalt, on the other hand, has an extremely low albedo, which is why a parking lot in July can burn your feet.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] The second factor is the shape of the city. Tall buildings placed close together form what are called urban canyons. Heat bounces back and forth between the walls and gets trapped, and the buildings also block the wind that would otherwise carry that warm air away.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [thoughtful] And third, there's what we call waste heat: the heat given off by human activity. You'd probably guess that traffic is the main source, and in a lot of cities, that's true. But in the case study I'll be referring to throughout today, which looked at a mid-sized city in Ontario, it wasn't vehicles that produced the most waste heat. It was industry, largely because of a cluster of factories right next to downtown. Air conditioning units came a fairly distant third.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [serious] Now, the effects. The most obvious one is on health. Heat waves kill more people in North America each year than any other type of weather event, and the elderly are especially at risk, because the body's ability to cool itself declines with age.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] But there's an economic side, too. When a city heats up, demand for electricity rises sharply, mainly because of all those air conditioners running at once, and utilities sometimes struggle to keep up. Natural gas use, by contrast, hardly changes at all in summer, so that isn't really where the costs come from.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [engaged] There's also an effect on water that's often overlooked. When rain falls on hot pavement and rooftops, the water warms up before it drains into streams and rivers. And that's a real problem for fish that depend on cold water. In the Ontario study, researchers recorded a sharp decline in trout in the streams below the city. [aside] Not salmon, interestingly; they'd disappeared from that river long before the city expanded, so it's trout that are now under pressure.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [brisk, transitioning] So, what can be done? Let's look at four approaches. The first is the cool roof. People tend to picture white roof tiles, but in fact most cool roofs are just ordinary roofs with a reflective coating applied on top, usually white or pale grey. It's cheap, it can go onto an existing building, and it can lower the surface temperature of a roof by thirty degrees or more.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [balanced] The second approach is the green roof, a roof planted with vegetation. Green roofs cool the air through evaporation, and they soak up rainwater, which helps reduce flooding. They're a lot more expensive than cool roofs, though, and many older buildings simply aren't strong enough to support the weight of wet soil.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [enthusiastic] The third approach, and probably the one residents like best, is planting street trees. But not all trees are equally useful. The key thing isn't how tall a tree grows. What really matters is having wide canopies, that's the spreading layer of branches and leaves that actually throws shade onto the street. A tall, narrow tree like a poplar does surprisingly little.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] In the Ontario city, the tree-planting program was interesting because of where it was targeted. You might expect planners to start with the oldest neighbourhoods, or with the downtown core, where it's hottest. Instead, they focused on districts where people had a low income, because those areas had the fewest trees to begin with, and residents there were the least likely to own air conditioners.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [measured] The fourth approach is the cool pavement: road and sidewalk surfaces that are made lighter in colour. These do work, but they've turned out to have an unexpected drawback. On bright days, the light reflected off them creates glare, which pedestrians find really uncomfortable, and some studies suggest they can actually make people walking on them feel hotter, not cooler.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [reflective] So why haven't these measures been adopted everywhere? You'd assume the main obstacle is the initial cost, and that's certainly an issue. But the city officials interviewed in the Ontario study said that wasn't really what held them back. The bigger problem, they said, was maintenance. Reflective coatings get dirty and gradually lose their effect, and young trees need regular watering for several years. The money for that kind of upkeep just isn't there in most budgets.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [wrapping up, brisk] Okay. Next week we'll look at how heat islands are measured, using satellite images and sensors mounted on buses. Please read chapter seven before then.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test. You now have two minutes to check your answers.

question_groups.heading: URBAN HEAT ISLANDS

items.prompt: Causes — The temperature difference between a city and the surrounding area is largest at ___
items.evidence: It's widest at night, because the city keeps releasing the heat
items.trap: Listeners may expect the afternoon, which the lecturer explicitly rejects.

items.prompt: Dark materials such as asphalt reflect little light: they have a low ___
items.evidence: Asphalt, on the other hand, has an extremely low albedo
items.trap: The prompt paraphrases 'absorb most of the sunlight'; fresh snow is an example of the opposite.

items.prompt: In the Ontario study, most waste heat came from ___
items.evidence: It was industry, largely because of a cluster of factories
items.trap: Traffic is the usual main source and air conditioning is mentioned as third.

items.prompt: Effects — Hot weather sharply increases the need for ___
items.evidence: When a city heats up, demand for electricity rises sharply
items.trap: Natural gas is mentioned but its use hardly changes.

items.prompt: Warm runoff has led to a fall in numbers of ___ in nearby streams
items.evidence: researchers recorded a sharp decline in trout in the streams below the city
items.trap: Salmon is mentioned but had disappeared long before.

items.prompt: Solutions — Cool roofs: usually a reflective ___ is added to a normal roof
items.evidence: ordinary roofs with a reflective coating applied on top
items.trap: White roof tiles are what people imagine, not what is usually used.

items.prompt: Street trees: the best species have broad ___
items.evidence: What really matters is having wide canopies
items.trap: Height is mentioned first and rejected; the plural form is spoken.

items.prompt: Ontario planting programme aimed at areas where residents' ___ was low
items.evidence: they focused on districts where people had a low income
items.trap: The oldest neighbourhoods and the downtown core are suggested and rejected.

items.prompt: Cool pavements: reflected light can cause ___, which people on foot dislike
items.evidence: the light reflected off them creates glare, which pedestrians find really uncomfortable
items.trap: Heat is also mentioned as a possible problem, but the gap requires what reflected light creates.

items.prompt: Officials see ___, not set-up costs, as the main barrier
items.evidence: The bigger problem, they said, was maintenance.
items.trap: Initial cost is the expected answer but officials say it wasn't the main problem; 'upkeep' is a synonym but the spoken word is maintenance.
